doc.title: Mose Allison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Not listening to his own records; classical listening over jazz
summary: Audre says he turned off his records and mainly listened to classical music after LSU.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: Do you listen back to your recordings, or did you used to do so?
If I had them...I don’t remember... You never did do that. If I was playing one of your albums when you came in, you’d say, “would you turn that off?”
Yeah. I never knew you to want to...
No. He never wanted... He always liked the live performance of it.
Dad, you said it never sounded like it felt or something.
Yeah. It never sounded like it felt.
I know a number of musicians who don’t like to listen back to themselves.
Another thing I remember you saying, when you began listening to classical music, I don’t think you ever listened to jazz or blues again. You always played classical music,
and you said everything that’s ever been done in music has been done in classical music.
When did you begin listening to classical music that seriously?
At LSU, I think.
Yes.
And then I don’t remember you ever buying any modern music after that.
Not even jazz records.
Well, I used to listen a lot when we got to New York, when we were living...
Live.
you’d be out on the scene.
No. On the radio.
Oh, on the radio. I forgot about the radio. But you never did buy them. I just remember the one you bought last was “Up ‘N Adam”...
Oh, Lester Young.
...by Lester Young.
That’s a 1950 or 1951 recording.
That’s right. That was right when we got married that you bought that.
